newsitem.title: USA: Dole starts marathon blitz in bid to win election.
newsitem.headline: Dole starts marathon blitz in bid to win election.

text.p: Republican Bob Dole kicks off on Friday an around-the-clock marathon blitz of up to 15 states in his last-ditch quest to oust President Bill Clinton from the White House.
From noon Friday to noon Tuesday, the 73-year-old candidate promised to "give it all I got" to win the election which, based on polls, Clinton is heavily favoured to win.

Dole's end-of-campaign tour goes from here to Cleveland and then to Grand Rapids, Mich., by plane. The campaign entourage then boards buses through small towns in Michigan, ending with an event in Detroit on Saturday morning at a 1 a.m. rally.

The caravan then flies to Newark, N.J., for a 4:30 a.m. rally. Then on to Philadelphia, Indianapolis, Covington, Ky., St. Louis, Omaha, Neb., Sioux Falls, S.D., and ending the grueling day at Grand Junction, Colo.

Sunday gets underway at 2:30 a.m. local time in the 24-hour western gambling capital of Las Vegas. He then heads for California with its rich prize of 54 of the 270 electoral votes needed to win on Tuesday.
In all, the Dole team has mapped out 15 possible states holding a total of 204 electoral votes.
When he announced the 96-hour trip on Thursday during a rally at Florida International University, the crowd roared their approval.
"The last time I fought 'round the clock for my country was in 1945, In Italy," Dole said, referring to his Second World War combat service when he was severely wounded.
"I will once again fight 'round the clock for America's future. Ninety-six hours of nonstop campaigning. From noon on Friday until noon on Nov. 5," said Dole.
"I am determined to make every hour of this decisive election count," he added. "The stakes are that high."
Dole was asked whether he would see a hotel room now and then.

"I think you have to get a little -- got to get some rest, you got to change, take a shower and clean up a little bit ... if we could rent our rooms by the hour, we could save a lot of money the next four days."
Dole, behind in double digits in most polls, might as well give it his all.

This is his third try for the presidency. The first two in 1980 and 1988 ended in failure when he did not get the Republican nomination. This is his last campaign, he said, and if he does not pull out the victory he wants then he planned to find a new career, perhaps working with fellow disabled people.
Clinton ended his successful 1992 campaign with a 30-hour trip that finished in Little Rock. Dole's trip ends in Russell, Kan., his hometown where he and his wife Elizabeth plan to vote.

Losing Democratic candidates -- George McGovern in 1972 and Michael Dukakis in 1988 -- also had extensive, virtually sleepless plane trips at the close of their campaigns, but not for anything like 96 straight hours.
